title: U.S. finalizes Section 301 tariffs on 60 countries over forced-labor rules
summary: The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative finalized Section 301 tariffs on 60 countries that have not sufficiently adopted and enforced import bans on goods made with forced labor. South Korea, along with the European Union, Japan, Taiwan and Switzerland, will face Section 301 tariffs on some products, capped at 10% or 12.5% including most-favored-nation tariff rates. A 10% tariff will apply to 17 countries that have enforced such import-ban systems or pledged to adopt them through reciprocal trade agreements, while the remaining countries under investigation will be subject to a 12.5% tariff. Raw materials that could create supply shortages in the United States, products that could disrupt the broader economy, and items that are difficult to source domestically in sufficient quantities at reasonable prices will be excluded from the tariff measures.

title: Thune says CLARITY Act unlikely to pass Senate before summer recess
summary: U.S. Senate Republican Majority Leader John Thune said the CLARITY Act appears unlikely to pass before the Senate’s summer recess. According to CoinDesk, the industry sees a high chance of the bill passing this year only if it makes meaningful progress by Aug. 7, the last effective legislative day before recess on the local calendar. Thune said he wants to begin the Senate’s review process for CLARITY at least before the summer break, which would preserve some chance of advancing the bill during the short remaining session in September even if it misses the key timeline. If it is pushed to September, however, the bill would have to compete for priority with other major legislation ahead of the midterm elections.

title: Fears of an AI-driven DeFi hacking disaster may be premature, experts say
summary: Concerns over AI-driven DeFi hacks are spreading, but those fears may be premature, according to Cointelegraph. Dragonfly managing partner Haseeb Qureshi said concerns about a wave of DeFi hacks are misguided, adding that even including the major hacking incident in April, monthly hacking losses this year have been declining and average annual losses have also been falling. Stephen Ajayi, chief offensive security engineer at blockchain security firm Hacken, said the main causes of Web3 losses are key compromises, infrastructure vulnerabilities and user error, adding that claims of a hacking disaster driven by AI are overstated.
